1.pericope_label: But in the last days it shall come to pass, that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established in the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills; and people shall flow unto it.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the opening a sudden transition from deepest gloom to light, reports the modern claim that this prophet is the original author of the three verses and refuses it as far too sweeping, and takes the elevation as spiritual, above all else visible and invisible; Keil and Delitzsch state the governing thought, Zion exalted from deepest degradation to highest glory, and set out the structure of the whole chapter.

Gill takes the adversative as marking dependence on what precedes and subdivides the last days, the first of them being the days of Christ in the flesh which were also the last days of the Jewish state; Calvin locates the change in the audience, the prophet turning aside from the whole people to the faithful few, and makes it a rule that threatenings must be moderated when the children of God are in view.

Clarke reports the judgment that this prophet borrowed the passage and offers two alternatives, refers the fulfilment to the coming of the Messiah, and cautions that the closing verses correspond only faintly to the Maccabean conquests to which they have been applied; Wesley alone anchors the words first in the return from captivity and only then in the founding of the church.

Henry works the contrast into the image of a phoenix rising from the ashes of the church, makes the coincidence with the other prophet the point so that the promises stand on two witnesses, and describes what is promised as a new charter with a new way of worship.

debates.question: Which prophet wrote these verses first?

positions.position: Either this prophet borrowed from the other, or the Spirit inspired both, or both copied a common original then current.
The preponderance of opinion favours this prophet, but the confident modern claim that no one now thinks otherwise is far too sweeping.
The question is beside the point: two prophets said the same thing at the same time so that the promise might stand on two witnesses.
The days of the Messiah, and specifically the last of them, the first having been the days of Christ in the flesh.
The expiring of the seventy years of captivity, literally fulfilled when the second temple was built and only spiritually when the church was founded.
The time of the Messiah's coming, when the Gentiles were admitted and the apostles preached from Jerusalem outwards.

outliers.claim: Makes the passage a rule for teaching, that terrors must be moderated when prophets and teachers have regard to the children of God, since the more a man is touched with the fear of God the more he dreads his judgment and is fearful enough already.

themes: But in the last days it shall come to pass, that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established in the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills; and people shall flow unto it.

2.pericope_label: And many nations shall come, and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for the law shall go forth of Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many people, and rebuke strong nations afar off; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the coming of the nations as preparing for more definite prophecies, asking the way in this world and finding the house in the eternal one, and sets the promise of peace against a present still rife with wars; Keil and Delitzsch add the caution that the race reaches this goal not through general humanitarian ideas and efforts but solely through the omnipotence and faithfulness of the Lord.

Gill notes the different word for the peoples in the parallel passage, reports the Jewish commentators who make the Messiah the judge, and takes the words afar off, absent from the parallel, of distant ages as well as distant lands; Calvin makes the word many decisive against the narrow borders of the old kingdom, argues that the kingdom promised is spiritual because tribute could be imposed where faith could not, and insists the submission is voluntary and not by the sword.

Wesley finds partial fulfilments in the proselyted servants who came up with their masters and in the released captives encouraging one another, and keeps the going forth of the law local to Jerusalem.

debates.question: Who is the judge among the nations?

positions.position: The King Messiah, on the authority of three Jewish commentators; or, on an impersonal reading, the church, the word and doctrine, or the Lord acting by the ministry of the word.
Certainly God himself, the verb meaning to rule, so that nations which had not obeyed him now own him as king.

debates.question: Where and when did the law go forth from Zion?

positions.position: Literally at the beginning of the gospel, first preached at Jerusalem; and the phrase is on the top of the mountains, not of a mountain, so the church was never confined to one place.
In Jerusalem the only way of worshipping God is declared, and from there the only law of right worship goes out.

outliers.claim: Distinguishes two respects of God's kingdom: he governs the devil and the wicked, but not by his word nor by the sanctifying power of his Spirit, so that they obey against their will, whereas his peculiar government is of his church only, where he bends hearts to follow him willingly.

themes: And many nations shall come, and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for the law shall go forth of Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.

And he shall judge among many people, and rebuke strong nations afar off; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.

4.pericope_label: But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid: for the mouth of the Lord of hosts hath spoken it. For all people will walk every one in the name of his god, and we will walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and ever.

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the proverb a historical reference in the security of the nation under Solomon, and explains the following verse by the blending of the near and distant futures in prophetic vision, as the destruction of the city is elsewhere described in terms finally accomplished at the judgment.

Gill pictures the security concretely, men sitting in their gardens and fields instead of locking themselves in walled towns, and takes the walking of the nations in their own names as describing the interval before the promise is fulfilled; Calvin asks why the vine and fig tree are named rather than the dwelling-house and answers that the point is exposure, and states and solves the apparent inconsistency between the two verses.

Clarke calls the phrase proverbial of perfect peace and notes that this verse is an addition to the prophecy as it stands in the parallel passage, and reads the following verse as the state of the Gentile world against a people that has worshipped one God since the captivity; Wesley makes the peace that of the redeemed from captivity and the walking of the nations a plain fact of custom.

debates.question: Why are the vine and the fig tree named rather than the house?

positions.position: Because the point is exposure: a man in the open fears no violence, since thieves will observe what is just, and may sleep in the open air and be safe.
Because they are proverbial of security and rural comfort, and are the representative trees of the country.

debates.question: How can all peoples walk in the name of their own gods when all nations were just said to come?

positions.position: The verse does not describe the promised age but supports the faithful until it arrives, so that they continue firm while the nations remain divided.
It describes the interval: until the promised times come the nations retain their former religion.
The near and distant futures are blended in the vision, the rule described applying primarily to the prosperity after the return.

outliers.claim: Observes that this verse is an addition to the prophecy as it stands in the parallel passage of the other prophet, and is not unworthy of him for beauty of imagery and elegance of expression.

themes: But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid: for the mouth of the Lord of hosts hath spoken it.
For all people will walk every one in the name of his god, and we will walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and ever.

6.pericope_label: In that day, saith the Lord, will I assemble her that halteth, and I will gather her that is driven out, and her that I have afflicted; And I will make her that halted a remnant, and her that was cast far off a strong nation: and the Lord shall reign over them in mount Zion from henceforth, even for ever. And thou, O tower of the flock, the strong hold of the daughter of Zion, unto thee shall it come, even the first dominion; the kingdom shall come to the daughter of Jerusalem.

schools.summary: Ellicott argues from the figure that the people being a flock their city is its tower or protection, and says outright that this is more satisfactory than the reading which puts the tower near Bethlehem; Keil and Delitzsch take the feminine forms as neuter and collective, read the limping as the condition of the dispersed, and place the promise structurally as the restoration of the throne founded by David.

Gill rejects the reading that makes the halting a wavering between God and idols, offers the lame and maimed sheep instead, and lays out four candidates for the tower without settling on one; Calvin derives the halting from a root meaning the side, calls the divided-allegiance reading foreign to the drift of the passage, prefers to take the tower as the city God chose to gather his people, and will not contend if another sense is preferred.

Clarke takes the halting as wavering between the true God and idols, quotes the Chaldee paraphrase applying the promise positively to a hidden Messiah, and identifies the first dominion with the divine theocracy under Christ; Wesley takes the halting as weakness under oppressing conquerors and distinguishes the type under the returned governor from the antitype in the Messiah's kingdom.

Henry settles on the city as the tower, the flock resorting there three times a year, and argues that the promised dominion by no means had its accomplishment under the governor of the return, whose rule matched it neither in splendour at home nor in power abroad.

positions.position: Wavering between the true God and idols, with captivity and affliction following from that idolatry.
Not that at all: lame and maimed sheep, or sinners who go sideways rather than uprightly.
Not that at all: the root means the side, so the sense is maimed or weak; the divided-allegiance reading is foreign to the passage.
The miserable condition of the dispersed, the forms being neuter and collective.

debates.question: What is the tower of the flock?

positions.position: Undecided among a place near Bethlehem, Bethlehem itself, a tower at the sheep gate, or the city.
The temple or Jerusalem, or both, as the stronghold of the people.
Jerusalem as the flock's tower or protection, which is more satisfactory than the place near Bethlehem.
The holy city, so called because God chose it to gather his people, the two clauses standing in apposition.

outliers.claim: Calls the Chaldee paraphrase remarkable here, since it applies the promise positively to the Messiah, addressing him as one hidden because of the sins of the congregation of Zion, to whom the kingdom shall come.

themes: In that day, saith the Lord, will I assemble her that halteth, and I will gather her that is driven out, and her that I have afflicted;
And I will make her that halted a remnant, and her that was cast far off a strong nation: and the Lord shall reign over them in mount Zion from henceforth, even for ever.
And thou, O tower of the flock, the strong hold of the daughter of Zion, unto thee shall it come, even the first dominion; the kingdom shall come to the daughter of Jerusalem.

9.pericope_label: Now why dost thou cry out aloud? is there no king in thee? is thy counsellor perished? for pangs have taken thee as a woman in travail. Be in pain, and labour to bring forth, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail: for now shalt thou go forth out of the city, and thou shalt dwell in the field, and thou shalt go even to Babylon; there shalt thou be delivered; there the Lord shall redeem thee from the hand of thine enemies.

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the intervening misery beside the vision of returned glory, and meets the naming of Babylon head on, observing that the prediction has caused difficulty to those who doubt that prophets can prophesy, since Babylon was not considered at all in this prophet's day; Keil and Delitzsch describe the same turn of the prophet's eye from the glorious future to the immediate one.

Gill attends to the doubled expression for the cry, a vehement lamentation raised as though the case were desperate; Calvin explains why contrary things are blended, gives the faithful leave to grieve since the strongest cannot look on such calamities without sorrow, and reads the repeated adverb as saying that even from the grave God will redeem.

Clarke answers the two questions as accusation, that the king is gone because they rejected the Lord their king and the counsellors' advice was rejected in the prophets; Wesley answers them as consolation, that their God is still their king and the Wonderful Counsellor has the conduct of their sufferings, and notes that the word for redeem denotes redemption by the next kinsman.
Henry draws the practical conclusion, that believers should cry aloud under distresses, but with the prayer of faith and not with despondency.

debates.question: How are the questions about the king and the counsellor to be taken?

positions.position: As accusation: there is no king because they rejected the Lord their king, and the counsellor's words were rejected in the prophets.
As consolation: the earthly king is lost but their God is still their king, and the Wonderful Counsellor remains with them.
As statement of fact: the king and counsellors of Jerusalem will be powerless to help in the emergency.

debates.question: What weight rests on the naming of Babylon?

positions.position: It is a difficulty for those who doubt that prophets can prophesy, since Babylon was not in view in this prophet's day and recovered its dignity only a century later; the prophet wrote it and the people did go.
It marks the deportation which must precede the glorification.

outliers.claim: Refuses to let the promise soften the prospect: God's care does not exempt the faithful from troubles, and they are exhorted to prepare to undergo them, being not only ejected from their country to wander like vagrants but led away as to their grave.

themes: Now why dost thou cry out aloud? is there no king in thee? is thy counsellor perished? for pangs have taken thee as a woman in travail.

Be in pain, and labour to bring forth, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail: for now shalt thou go forth out of the city, and thou shalt dwell in the field, and thou shalt go even to Babylon; there shalt thou be delivered; there the Lord shall redeem thee from the hand of thine enemies.

11.pericope_label: Now also many nations are gathered against thee, that say, Let her be defiled, and let our eye look upon Zion. But they know not the thoughts of the Lord, neither understand they his counsel: for he shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor. Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion: for I will make thine horn iron, and I will make thy hoofs brass: and thou shalt beat in pieces many people: and I will consecrate their gain unto the Lord, and their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth.

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses the enemies' looking as contemplating the destruction with pleasure, compares the message to the Assyrian king who was told he was only an instrument, and prefers the reading of the old versions which puts the final promise in the second person; Keil and Delitzsch give the verses plainly without comment.

Gill rules out both the Assyrian siege and the Babylonian conquest as the gathering meant, since neither army was threshed by Zion, and draws the rule that men know their own designs but not the Lord's; Calvin takes the horn for strength, cites a Jewish paraphrase, and makes the command to arise emphatic because the church had lain prostrate like a dead body and raising the dead is God's peculiar office.

Clarke identifies the gathering with the Chaldeans and the neighbouring peoples, explains the iron horns and brazen hoofs as unconquerable strength, and asks whether the consecration was not fulfilled in the restoring of the sacred vessels; Wesley reads the first person in the last promise as the church speaking of the spoils of her conquered enemies.

debates.question: Which gathering of nations is meant?

positions.position: The Chaldeans and the surrounding peoples who rejoiced at the city's overthrow.
Neither the Assyrian siege nor the Chaldean conquest, since neither army was threshed by Zion; rather the times of the Maccabees, with the gospel age and the last battle also proposed.
God: the gain taken shall be restored and consecrated, as when the sacred vessels were given back.
Zion herself: the old versions give the second person, thou shalt consecrate their gain.
The church, speaking in the first person of the spoils of her conquered enemies.

outliers.claim: Makes the command to arise emphatic on the ground that the church had been cast down so as to lie prostrate like a dead body without feeling, so that God rouses her by his voice alone, raising the dead being his peculiar office, from which the faithful may take heart when no strength remains in them.

themes: Now also many nations are gathered against thee, that say, Let her be defiled, and let our eye look upon Zion.
But they know not the thoughts of the Lord, neither understand they his counsel: for he shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor.

Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion: for I will make thine horn iron, and I will make thy hoofs brass: and thou shalt beat in pieces many people: and I will consecrate their gain unto the Lord, and their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth.
